description: Major bones of the skeleton, the six functions of the skeleton and how the skeletal system supports physical activity.
content_html:
The Framework of Movement

The human skeleton is a living structure made of 206 bones that provides the framework for every movement you make in sport. Without it, muscles would have nothing to pull against. The skeleton works in partnership with the muscular system: muscles contract and pull on bones, which act as levers, creating movement at joints. Understanding which bones are where — and what they do — underpins everything else in PE.

Bones of the Skeleton: Head to Toe

Working from the top of the body downwards, the cranium sits at the very top of the head, curving down around the brain. Below it, the vertebrae form a column of 33 bones running from the base of the skull to the pelvis — protecting the spinal cord and giving the trunk both stability and a controlled range of movement. At the front of the chest, the sternum (breastbone) and the ribs form the ribcage, encasing the heart and lungs. The clavicle (collarbone) connects the sternum to the shoulder on each side, and the flat, triangular scapula (shoulder blade) lies across the upper back.

The humerus is the long bone of the upper arm, running from the shoulder joint down to the elbow. Together, the scapula and humerus form the shoulder joint — a ball-and-socket joint that allows the greatest range of movement in the body. At the elbow, three bones meet: the humerus, the radius (which runs along the thumb side of the forearm) and the ulna (which runs along the little-finger side). In the wrist and hand, the carpals form the wrist, the metacarpals form the palm, and the phalanges are the finger bones. These hand bones are named explicitly in the OCR specification and are examined directly — learn all three.

Moving to the lower body, the pelvis is a large basin-shaped structure at the base of the spine. It forms the hip joint with the head of the femur — a ball-and-socket joint allowing the greatest range of movement in the lower limb. At the knee, the femur articulates with the tibia (the large shin bone), forming a hinge joint. The patella sits in front of the knee joint. The fibula runs alongside the tibia on the outer side of the lower leg. At the foot, the tarsals form the ankle and heel, the metatarsals form the arch of the foot, and the phalanges are the toe bones — mirroring the hand structure.

Key Fact

OCR’s 19 named bones: cranium, vertebrae, ribs, sternum, clavicle, scapula, pelvis, humerus, ulna, radius, carpals, metacarpals, phalanges (hand), femur, patella, tibia, fibula, tarsals, metatarsals. The hand and foot bones (carpals, metacarpals, phalanges, tarsals, metatarsals) are OCR-specific additions — make sure you can name and locate all of them.

The Six Functions of the Skeleton

The skeleton does far more than hold the body upright. It serves six distinct functions, each of which can be applied directly to sport and physical activity.

Support — the skeleton holds the body upright against gravity. A sprinter’s lower limbs support their entire body weight as they drive off the blocks. Without a rigid skeletal frame, the muscular system would have nothing to act on.

Posture — the vertebral column and pelvis maintain the upright alignment of the body. Good posture keeps the skeleton in correct mechanical alignment, reducing injury risk and allowing muscles to work most efficiently. A rower must maintain an upright spine throughout the drive phase; poor posture transfers force inefficiently and risks back injury. OCR lists posture as a distinct function, separate from support — always treat them as two separate marks.

Protection — flat bones protect vital organs. The cranium shields the brain; the ribs and sternum form a cage around the heart and lungs. In contact sports such as rugby, the ribcage absorbs impact forces that would otherwise damage the heart and lungs directly.

Movement — bones act as levers. When the biceps contracts during a bicep curl, the forearm bones (radius and ulna) pivot at the elbow to lift the load. In kicking a football, the femur swings at the hip and the tibia swings at the knee, producing explosive leg extension.

Blood cell production — red bone marrow inside flat and irregular bones produces red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets. Red blood cells carry oxygen to the working muscles during exercise via haemoglobin. This function links directly to cardiovascular performance: a well-functioning skeletal system supports oxygen delivery to muscles.

Storage of minerals — bones store calcium and phosphorus. These minerals are released into the bloodstream when the body needs them, and weight-bearing exercise stimulates the bones to increase their mineral density, making them stronger over time.

Key Fact

The six functions of the skeleton are: support, posture, protection, movement, blood cell production and storage of minerals. Each one links to sporting performance — for example, the femur acts as a lever during kicking (movement), the ribs protect the lungs during a tackle (protection), and the vertebral column maintains alignment during a rowing drive (posture).

A very common error is to list only five functions and miss posture entirely, or to treat posture and support as the same thing. In OCR, they are explicitly two separate functions. Support is about bearing the weight of the body against gravity — the skeleton stops you collapsing. Posture is about maintaining correct alignment and shape during movement — the spine and pelvis keep the body in the optimal mechanical position for efficient performance and injury prevention. In an exam, if you write “support/posture” as one combined answer, you will likely receive credit for only one function. Always list them separately and give a different sporting example for each.

OCR explicitly requires students to name and locate the carpals, metacarpals, phalanges (hand), tarsals and metatarsals in addition to the major long bones. These bones matter in sport: the carpals and metacarpals absorb force during a gymnast’s handstand or a goalkeeper’s diving save; the metatarsals and tarsals form the arch of the foot, which distributes body weight during running and jumping. A question asking “name the bones of the hand” expects all three groups: carpals (wrist), metacarpals (palm) and phalanges (fingers).
exam_tip_html: On a 3-mark ‘Describe’ question about skeletal functions, name a function, explain what it means, and apply it to a sport — that’s the three marks. On a 6-mark ‘Analyse’ question, avoid listing functions as bullet points. Instead, write in continuous prose: state the function, explain how it works, and link it to a named sporting movement. OCR’s key difference from other boards is the inclusion of posture as a separate, sixth function — always list it separately from support and use a different sport example. If asked to name bones at a joint, state both (or all three) bones: the knee joint involves the femur and tibia; the elbow involves the humerus, radius and ulna. Failing to name all articulating bones costs marks on identify-the-bones questions.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • OCR requires 19 named bones, including the hand bones (carpals, metacarpals, phalanges) and foot bones (tarsals, metatarsals) in addition to the major long bones — learn all 19 and their locations.
  • The six functions of the skeleton are support, posture, protection, movement, blood cell production and storage of minerals — OCR lists posture as a distinct function, so always treat it separately from support in exam answers.
  • Each function can be linked directly to sporting performance: levers for movement, ribcage for protection in contact sport, bone marrow producing red blood cells that carry oxygen to working muscles during aerobic exercise.

practice_questions.text: Name the bone that sits in front of the knee joint.
Define the term 'blood cell production' as a function of the skeleton.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for stating that red bone marrow produces blood cells; 1 mark for specifying red blood cells (which carry oxygen to working muscles during exercise) or white blood cells / platelets.

practice_questions.text: Describe how two of the six functions of the skeleton help a rugby player during a match.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correctly naming a valid function (e.g. protection); 1 mark for explaining that function physiologically (e.g. the ribs and sternum form a cage that shields the heart and lungs from impact forces during a tackle); 1 mark for a second distinct function applied to rugby (e.g. movement — the femur and tibia act as levers at the hip and knee, producing the explosive leg drive of a sprint). Accept any two of: support, posture, protection, movement, blood cell production, storage of minerals, each with a relevant rugby application.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the skeleton provides the function of posture during physical activity, and why this is different from the function of support.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for explaining posture: the vertebral column and pelvis keep the body in correct mechanical alignment during movement; 1 mark for applying posture to sport (e.g. a rower must maintain spinal alignment throughout the drive to transfer force efficiently and avoid injury); 1 mark for explaining support: the skeleton bears the weight of the body against gravity so the body does not collapse; 1 mark for clearly distinguishing between them (support is about resisting gravity/bearing load; posture is about maintaining the correct shape and alignment for efficient and safe movement).

practice_questions.text: State two bones that are named in the OCR specification but were NOT required by other GCSE exam boards, and state where each is located in the body.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each of any two OCR-specific bones with correct location: carpals (wrist / wrist bones), metacarpals (palm of the hand), phalanges (fingers / toes — accept either location), tarsals (ankle / heel bones), metatarsals (arch of the foot / foot bones between ankle and toes). Two marks awarded for two different bones each with a correct location.

practice_questions.text: A county-level hockey player relies on her skeleton for a range of functions during a match. Analyse how two functions of the skeleton contribute to her performance during the game.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two functions clearly identified and developed with accurate physiological explanation, each applied specifically to hockey performance. The candidate links structure to function (e.g. how the femur acts as a lever at the hip during a reverse hit; how red blood cells produced in bone marrow carry oxygen to support sustained aerobic play) and demonstrates understanding of how skeletal function supports overall performance throughout.

Secure: Two functions identified with mostly accurate explanation and applied to a general sporting context. Some links between structure and performance may be undeveloped.

Developing: One or two functions mentioned with limited development. Application to sport is vague or missing from one function.

Emerging: Basic naming of functions with little or no explanation or sporting application.

Acceptable content: movement (long bones as levers; femur pivots at the hip to produce the sweeping action of a reverse hit); protection (ribcage protects heart and lungs from stick or ball impact); posture (vertebral column maintains alignment when the player bends to receive a low ball); mineral storage (calcium stored in the skeleton maintains bone density under the repeated loading of running); blood cell production (red blood cells produced in bone marrow carry oxygen to working muscles during aerobic play).

knowledge_checks.q: Which two bones form the shoulder joint?
Which function of the skeleton is responsible for producing red blood cells?
The _____ sits in front of the knee joint and protects it.
OCR names _____ as a separate sixth function of the skeleton, distinct from support.
Match each bone group to its location in the body:

flashcard_questions.q: What type of joint is found at the shoulder and which bones form it?
flashcard_questions.a: Ball-and-socket joint formed by the scapula and humerus, allowing movement in all directions.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the three bones that meet at the elbow joint.
flashcard_questions.a: Humerus (upper arm), radius (thumb side of forearm) and ulna (little-finger side of forearm).

flashcard_questions.q: Which skeletal function directly supports oxygen delivery to muscles during aerobic exercise?
flashcard_questions.a: Blood cell production — red bone marrow makes red blood cells that carry oxygen via haemoglobin.

flashcard_questions.q: What does mineral storage in the skeleton involve?
flashcard_questions.a: Bones store calcium and phosphorus, which are released into the bloodstream when needed.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the function of flat bones such as the cranium and ribs?
flashcard_questions.a: Protection of vital organs — cranium protects the brain; ribs and sternum protect the heart and lungs.

flashcard_questions.q: How is posture different from support as a function of the skeleton?
flashcard_questions.a: Support bears body weight against gravity; posture maintains correct mechanical alignment during movement.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the three bone groups in the hand in order from wrist to fingertip.
Name the three bone groups in the foot in order from ankle to toe.
What is the femur and why is it important in sport?
flashcard_questions.a: The longest and strongest bone in the body; acts as the primary lever at the hip and knee for running, jumping and kicking.

flashcard_questions.q: The patella sits in front of the knee — what is its function?
flashcard_questions.a: Protects the knee joint and improves the mechanical efficiency of the quadriceps.

flashcard_questions.q: What connects muscles to bones at attachment points?
flashcard_questions.a: Tendons transmit muscular force to the skeleton, enabling movement.

flashcard_questions.q: Which bones form the hip joint and what type of joint is it?
flashcard_questions.a: Pelvis and femur form the hip joint — a ball-and-socket joint allowing the greatest range of movement in the lower limb.

glossary_terms.definition: Rigid bars that pivot around a fixed point (fulcrum) to produce movement when a force is applied.
The dome-shaped bone that forms the protective casing of the brain.
The eight small bones of the wrist that allow the fine, controlled movements of the hand.
The longest and strongest bone in the body, running from the hip to the knee and acting as the primary lever for running, jumping and kicking.
The kneecap; a small sesamoid bone that sits in front of the knee joint, protecting it and improving the mechanical efficiency of the quadriceps.
The iron-containing protein in red blood cells that binds to oxygen in the lungs and transports it to body tissues.
The function of the skeleton that maintains correct mechanical alignment of the body during movement, reducing injury risk and allowing efficient force transfer.
The five long bones forming the arch of the foot, connecting the tarsals to the toes.
